name: Streetwear / techwear style

lead: Streetwear is a casual style drawing on sportswear, skateboarding, surf culture, punk, hip-hop and Japanese street fashion, and it spread worldwide in the 1990s. Techwear and gorpcore apply technical outdoor apparel, such as puffer jackets, fleeces, hiking boots and cargo pants, to everyday city dress. The payoff is a current, trend-aware look.
Many labels build demand through limited releases, which has fed a resale market. Research has not tested whether these styles change how attractive a person is rated.

paras: People choose garments, silhouettes and brands that match the aesthetic. Streetwear leans on graphic pieces, sneakers and limited drops; techwear on functional shells, pockets and looser fits.
No health risks are documented. Commentators note the cost, hype-driven resale markets and cultural appropriation debates around the style.

angle.text: Hip-hop, skate and outdoor-gear-derived clothes make you look current and part of a style scene, and the look is visible as soon as you wear it. It is a style choice with no studies on attractiveness effects.

lead: Streetwear is a casual clothing style that spread worldwide in the 1990s, drawing on sportswear, skateboarding, surf culture, punk, hip-hop and Japanese street fashion.[1] Many labels build demand through limited releases and restricted supply, which has fed a resale market.[1]

Techwear and the related trend called gorpcore apply technical outdoor apparel to everyday urban dress. Gorpcore, a term coined in 2017 by writer Jason Chen, describes functional outdoor pieces such as puffer jackets, fleeces, hiking boots and cargo pants worn as street style.[2] Wikipedia links gorpcore to techwear as a related category.[2]

In appearance-focused communities these styles are discussed as aesthetic choices within clothing and personal style. No published studies have examined whether streetwear or techwear changes how attractive a person is rated.

paras: Streetwear is usually traced to New York hip-hop communities of the late 1970s and early 1980s, then absorbed Los Angeles surf and skate influences.[1] Sneaker collecting, branded T-shirts and limited drops became central features.[1]

Techwear and gorpcore emphasise functional garments: weather-resistant shells, pockets, utility accessories and looser fits, often from outdoor brands such as The North Face, Patagonia and Arc'teryx.[2]

Harlem designer Dapper Dan, whose boutique opened in 1982, is often described as an early figure mixing luxury logos with custom pieces.[1] In the 1980s Shawn Stussy began selling printed T-shirts and limited their distribution; record labels and artists later launched apparel lines such as Phat Farm, Sean John and Rocawear.[1]

In the 2010s Japanese labels and brands such as Supreme collaborated with luxury houses, and designers including Virgil Abloh brought streetwear into high fashion.[1] The term gorpcore appeared in 2017, and the Gucci and The North Face collaboration was announced in September 2021.[2]

Streetwear is widely described as a form of self-expression tied to African American culture, hip-hop and R&B.[1] Critics cited in the article argue its commercialisation raises cultural appropriation questions, and that resale and hype-driven buying prioritises profit over style.[1]
